entries.title: Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know
entries.summary: A CNN report quoting unnamed US officials alleges Tehran is developing plans for an attack on officials in Washington.
entries.content:
A CNN report quoting unnamed US officials alleges Tehran is developing plans for an attack on officials in Washington, DC.

CNN has reported that United States intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior officials in President Donald Trump’s administration with a “dirty bomb” or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC. The broadcaster quotes seven unnamed US officials.

However, the report sets out no evidence to support the claims.

According to CNN, its sources described the planning as an effort by Tehran to give itself options, not as an imminent attack. One source said US intelligence had picked up Iranian “chatter” indicating that bomb-making materials had been stashed inside the US. That claim has not been independently verified.

The White House said it was “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time, there are no credible threats to the homeland”. Iran’s mission to the United Nations said Tehran “categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations”.

The report was released as talks to end the US-Israel war on Iran have stalled and Trump said last week that Washington does not “need” a deal. The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt has just arrived in the region, bringing the number of US carriers there to three and adding to fears of a renewed escalation.

So what is a dirty bomb? Could Iran build one? And how seriously should the latest claims be taken?

What is a ‘dirty bomb’?

A dirty bomb, technically known as a radiological dispersal device, combines conventional explosives, such as dynamite, with radioactive material. When the bomb explodes, the resulting blast scatters the radioactive material into the surrounding area.

Unlike a nuclear weapon, a dirty bomb does not need enriched uranium or a nuclear chain reaction. The radioactive material can come from medical or industrial equipment, such as machines used in hospitals and research facilities. That makes a dirty bomb far cheaper and easier to build than a nuclear device. It is also far less destructive.

The main health risk comes from breathing in contaminated dust near the blast. As the material spreads, it becomes less concentrated and less harmful. The damage depends on the size of the explosive charge, the type and amount of radioactive material and the weather, especially the wind.

According to the US National Academy of Sciences, most dirty bombs would immediately contaminate an area of one or two city blocks although wind could carry radioactive particles over a few square miles.

Experts said dirty bombs are unlikely to cause mass casualties. In testimony to the US Senate in 2002, Richard Meserve, then-chairman of the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, estimated that deaths in most scenarios would be in the tens, not the hundreds or thousands.

“It’s important to understand that a dirty bomb isn’t an off-the-shelf nuclear bomb. There aren’t any mushroom clouds and massive shockwaves tearing down buildings and killing hundreds of thousands of people in the blink of an eye,” Talha Abdulrazaq, a researcher at the University of Exeter’s Strategy and Security Institute told Al Jazeera. “Instead, its primary effect would be psychological panic and hysteria in the target state alongside radioactive contamination, turning the area hit into a no-go zone.”

That is why experts call dirty bombs “weapons of mass disruption” rather than weapons of mass destruction.

Does Iran have the ability to build one?

In theory, yes. But so do many states and armed groups.

A dirty bomb is “really easy to make”, Scott Roecker, vice president for nuclear materials security at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, told Al Jazeera in 2022. Radioactive sources used in medicine and industry can be found in many countries and building a crude device does not require advanced technical knowledge.

Iran has a large civilian nuclear programme. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency’s last assessment, it held about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent as of June 2025.

In an April analysis for the European Council on Foreign Relations, Jacek Siewiera, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote that although the stockpile falls short of what is needed for a nuclear weapon, it “could be extraordinarily dangerous from a radiological and sabotage perspective”. He warned that a dirty bomb could be “either a deliberate element of escalation or an unintended consequence of weakened central control” because international institutions no longer know who controls Iran’s nuclear storage sites.

But even enriched uranium is only weakly radioactive, which makes it a poor choice for a dirty bomb. Many analysts also argued that Tehran would be unlikely to waste material it spent decades producing.

A June 2025 analysis by Chris Kremidas-Courtney for the Euro-Atlantic Resilience Centre, a Bucharest-based think tank, reached a similar conclusion.

Iran is “widely believed to have access to sufficient radioactive material for use in dirty bombs, particularly from civilian nuclear and industrial sources”, he wrote. He pointed to isotopes such as caesium-137, used in cancer treatment, and cobalt-60, used in industrial radiography.

Kremidas-Courtney, however, described a dirty bomb as a possible “tool of last resort under extreme circumstances”. He also judged that the US “poses a high bar for direct infiltration” and ports and maritime chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz, were more plausible targets.

Building a dirty bomb “is actually far easier than a conventional nuclear weapon” and does not require highly enriched uranium, Abdulrazaq said. Even after US strikes on the Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities, “a degraded capability doesn’t mean a destroyed capability,” he told Al Jazeera. “Iran certainly has access to all the components and expertise required to construct something as rudimentary as a dirty bomb.”

Iran “doesn’t have the missile or drone capability to strike US targets 10,000km [6,200 miles] and more away”, Abdulrazaq said. Therefore, any attack on Washington, DC, would almost certainly rely on clandestine smuggling networks or links to organised crime.

Even if Iran has the technical means, there is little public evidence that it has any ambition to build a dirty bomb, let alone set one off on US soil. Abdulrazaq said using a radiological weapon “would instantly destroy Iran’s remaining diplomatic credit” and would likely lead to an invasion and the collapse of its government.

“I highly doubt Iranian strategists are unaware of this reality, so the likelihood of a dirty bomb remains infinitesimally remote.”

How real is the threat?

According to CNN’s sources, US officials are divided on this point. One source said officials were debating whether Iran even had the personnel in place to carry out such an attack. The report also said there is no evidence that Tehran has decided to go ahead.

Iran does have a record of plotting against US officials. US prosecutors charged an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps operative in 2024 over an alleged murder-for-hire plot against Trump. But CNN noted that such plotting has mostly focused on opportunities to target officials while they travel abroad.

The latest report followed a series of US media stories about alleged Iranian plots. In October, the Axios news website and The New York Times reported on a memo from the director of national intelligence warning that Iranian plots against US personnel abroad had reached “advanced stages”. One official said some Iranian operatives may already be active inside the US. The memo did not identify specific targets or methods.

Critics said such reports, which often quote anonymous officials, risk building public support for escalation at a time when the war is deeply unpopular. In October, a Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey found that nearly 70 percent of respondents said the war was not worth fighting.

Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei dismissed the CNN report as baseless. In a post on X, he suggested the claims were meant to frighten the public and build support for further hostile action against Iran.

Abdulrazaq noted that the claims came from “a US intelligence assessment rather than a direct threat made by Tehran”. “The Iraq war in 2003 and the lies surrounding Iraqi WMDs [weapons of mass destruction] is sufficient enough to doubt publicly communicated intelligence assessments in a wartime information environment,” he said.

He added that a dirty bomb attack would “hand-deliver the political rationale” for a major US war on Iran, including a ground invasion, with bipartisan support even after Democrats take control of Congress in January. “Iranian strategists aren’t stupid, and if I’m telling you this, they surely have made similar assessments, so I highly doubt the veracity of these intelligence reports,” he said.

Has the US gone to war on faulty intelligence before?

Yes. One example is Iraq.

Before the 2003 invasion, President George W Bush’s administration argued that Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction and links to al-Qaeda. In February 2003, Secretary of State Colin Powell made the US government’s case to the United Nations Security Council, including claims that Iraq had mobile biological weapons laboratories.

No stockpiles were found after the US-led invasion was carried out. In 2005, a presidential commission concluded that US intelligence on Iraq’s weapons had been “dead wrong”. Much of the case rested on unreliable sources, including an Iraqi defector codenamed “Curveball”, whose claims about mobile labs proved to be fabricated.

The media also came under scrutiny. In 2004, The New York Times published an editors’ note acknowledging that some of its pre-war coverage, much of it based on unnamed officials and Iraqi exiles, had not been as rigorous as it should have been.

Four decades earlier, two reported attacks on US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin that the US government had said were unprovoked were used to justify a major US escalation in Vietnam. However, North Vietnam carried out the first attack in 1964 after US raids on its coast, and later evidence showed the second reported North Vietnamese attack two days later most likely never happened.

Have dirty bombs ever been used?

No successful dirty bomb attack has ever been recorded.

In 1995, Chechen fighters planted a container of radioactive caesium in Moscow’s Izmailovsky Park, but it never detonated. In 1998, a container of radioactive material rigged with explosives was discovered and defused near a railway line in Chechnya.

There have been other scares. In 2002, US authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of plotting a dirty bomb attack though he was never charged. In 2013, a truck carrying radioactive cobalt-60 from a hospital was stolen in Mexico, prompting UN warnings that the material could be used in a dirty bomb.

In 2022, Russia accused Ukraine of preparing to set off a dirty bomb and blame Moscow. Western governments dismissed the claim as “transparently false”.

entries.title: US senators demand FAA pause upgrades linked to nationwide ground stop
entries.summary: Thousands of routers used in communications systems are slated to be replaced, raising the risk of more problems.
entries.content:
Thousands of routers used in communications systems are slated to be replaced, raising the risk of more problems.

A group of Democratic Senators has asked the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to pause its plan to replace thousands of routers until an investigation is completed into why one such upgrade caused a national ground stop last week.

“With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding ‌‌safety ‌‌and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” the 13 senators wrote in a letter to the agency on Tuesday.

The FAA ordered all flights to remain grounded on Friday for about four hours, causing more than 10,000 flights to be cancelled and prompting ripple effects that continue to disrupt air travel in the US. It was only the second time the agency had issued such a sweeping order since the September 11, 2001 attacks.

The FAA said in a statement on Sunday that its initial investigation pointed to upgrades at two locations – a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas – as being the cause of the problem.

L3Harris, the agency’s network service provider, had been working to replace old copper wires with fibre-optic lines and to replace old routers with new ones made by Juniper Networks.

The FBI said on Tuesday that it was working with the Department of Transportation, the FAA, and L3Harris to investigate the incident, but had not taken possession of any equipment itself.

In their letter to the FAA, the group of senators asked the agency to halt plans to replace more than 3,000 additional routers.

“Based on information ⁠⁠provided to our offices from L3Harris, the copper-to-fibre transition involves converting 3,648 routers to Juniper ⁠⁠devices. To date, it is our understanding that ⁠⁠400 devices have ⁠⁠been installed, and 69 are operational,” wrote the lawmakers from the Senate Commerce Committee, ‌‌led by Maria Cantwell.

On Sunday, the FAA said the upgrades had started a long time ago.

“This type of work has been going on for years to transition from old copper wires that are being disconnected due to their obsolescence,” the FAA said on Sunday. The network became unstable, and data began flooding other equipment, causing problems with aircraft communications and radar feeds, leading the agency to order a halt to flights.

“I want the American people to know my number one job is to keep them safe,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy told ABC on Sunday. “So if we see these inconsistencies in the network, whether it’s communication with air traffic controllers and pilots, or with data feeds, we’re going to keep you safe.”

The White House has asked Congress for $50bn to complete an overhaul of the FAA’s technical infrastructure. Democratic lawmakers have said the administration was already authorised to use $12.5bn last year, but had only used a fraction of that so far.

entries.title: Bessent vs Lutnick: Who is winning the China chip debate?
entries.summary: A rift has emerged in Trump’s cabinet over China’s access to advanced AI chips as export controls tighten.
entries.content:
Trump avoids picking sides between feuding cabinet members, but US tightens chip restrictions on Beijing days before his summit with Xi.

A rift between United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over sales of advanced computer chips to China has spilled into public view.

On Monday, the administration of President Donald Trump introduced new rules requiring licences to sell advanced chips to buyers in named third countries suspected of being conduits to China. The new restrictions were written by Bessent’s Department of the Treasury and the White House – not Lutnick’s Department of Commerce, which usually oversees chip exports.

Trump, who is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, has so far not taken a side.

As the US reels from the resignation of chip maker Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang last week over revelations that he had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, here’s what this all means.

What is this dispute about?

The two cabinet members, who are both veteran investors, disagree over how strictly the US should limit China’s access to the advanced chips that power artificial intelligence (AI).

The US restricts exports of certain advanced AI chips to China. In December 2025, Trump announced that Nvidia could sell its H200 chip to approved Chinese customers, on condition that 25 percent of the revenue would go to the US government. In January, the administration relaxed licensing rules for the H200 and similar chips.

On Monday, new controls were issued to monitor access to US chips in Southeast Asia and Brazil – penned by Bessent with the backing of the National Security Council, not by Lutnick.

As commerce secretary, Lutnick oversees these export controls and is charged with determining which critical technologies US companies can sell abroad, with an eye towards national security.

He has been one of the administration’s most vocal supporters of allowing Nvidia, the world’s dominant maker of AI super chips, to sell to China, despite the fact that it is racing against the US to dominate development of the AI industry.

“You want to sell the Chinese enough that their developers get addicted to the American technology stack,” Lutnick said in July 2025.

But US rules still bar the most advanced chips from being sold to China, and reports of restricted Nvidia chips allegedly being smuggled into the country through unofficial routes have put Lutnick’s role under the microscope.

Lutnick’s department was accused of turning a blind eye to such smuggling and stalling a planned crackdown on actors thought to be involved.

Fellow cabinet members and lawmakers have questioned his department’s handling of the issue, and some lawmakers say it has undermined US national security.

Bessent has pressed for tougher enforcement of existing export rules.

“We have all the authorities that we need. They just need to be implemented,” he said on Friday.

The two men have been rivals for some time. In 2024, Elon Musk and other Trump allies lobbied for Lutnick to get the Treasury job, but it ultimately went to Bessent.

What happened at Nvidia?

Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for the most advanced chips used for AI. Worth trillions of dollars, it is among the world’s most valuable companies, and its customers include tech giants Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta.

Nvidia’s cofounder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, whom some US officials have suspected of working for Chinese intelligence – a claim denied by China.

Alice Huang is a former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that builds data centres in Southeast Asia which cater for Chinese clients.

Megaspeed bought more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips in about two years, but US authorities suspect that many of these chips were then smuggled into China rather than used in Megaspeed’s data centres, a charge it denies.

On Friday, Bessent said four government agencies, including the Treasury, had pushed for months to put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, but Lutnick’s Commerce Department had not acted.

“Commerce has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

He also questioned whether Nvidia had properly vetted its customers.

“The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said.

What are the new rules?

The new rules require companies to obtain a US licence before shipping advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries Washington suspects of acting as conduit routes for chips to reach China.

It also requires any data centre in the world using Nvidia chips to obtain Washington’s permission before it can “rent” computer power to Chinese customers. This closes a loophole that previously allowed Chinese companies to “rent” the use of advanced chips without purchasing them outright.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the restrictions as “economic coercion” and said Beijing would take “necessary measures” in response.

In Washington, the new restrictions were welcomed by John Moolenaar, the Republican chair of the House Select Committee on China.

The committee, a panel of lawmakers focused on competition with China’s ruling Communist Party, is one of the most hawkish voices on Beijing in Congress. Moolenaar criticised the administration’s decision last year to ease curbs on Nvidia’s chip sales to China.

“Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy,” he said.

Who else has weighed in on the row?

Senior officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have argued for keeping the most advanced chips out of China, while lawmakers from both parties have criticised Lutnick.

“It would be dumb and stupid for us to sell that to anybody, especially a country that’s going to reverse-engineer it and leapfrog us,” Rubio said in May.

Greer made a similar case last week, saying that US “crown jewels” should remain in US hands or in the hands of allies.

David Sacks, Trump’s former AI adviser, however, defended selling chips to China and dismissed those pushing for tighter controls.

“The policy of the China hawks is effectively the policy of the CCP [Chinese Communist Party]. Neither one wants American chips in China,” he said in a podcast appearance on Saturday.

On the other side of the political aisle, some Democrats have called for Lutnick to step down from his position for his failure to police chip smuggling.

“Making powerful Nvidia chips available to China through an apparent spy undercut both national security and economic competitiveness,” Senator Richard Blumenthal said in a post on X.

Both Lutnick and Jensen Huang have been summoned to testify before the Senate on December 3.

Where does Trump stand?

Trump has swung between restricting and allowing Nvidia’s sales to China. In April 2025, the White House curbed sales of the H20, a chip Nvidia made for the Chinese market – only to agree to allow them three months later.

His later decision in December to permit sales of the more powerful H200 marked a further easing of those restrictions.

Trump has stood by Lutnick, saying on Monday that he was not planning to remove him, days after the Reuters news agency reported that top White House aides had debated whether he should go.

Trump has acknowledged that the issue is splitting his cabinet, without explicitly taking sides.

“It’s a different viewpoint. One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Trump said. “They both are acceptable, but they are different views.”

Trump has also said it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia.

Trump and Xi are due to meet in Shenzhen on Thursday, during this week’s APEC summit. Ahead of their last meeting, when Xi visited the US in September, Washington banned imports of Chinese-made humanoid robots and threatened to sanction Chinese AI firms.

entries.title: Ghost Towns of Afghanistan: The Environmental Toll of Decades of War
entries.summary: A father confronts the aftermath of environmental damage from years of war in Afghanistan.
entries.content:
Witness

Ghost Towns of Afghanistan: The Environmental Toll of Decades of War

A father confronts the aftermath of environmental damage from years of war in Afghanistan.

Ibrahim, a father living in Kabul, returns to his home in Nangarhar province on Afghanistan’s eastern border with Pakistan to revisit a place transformed by war, displacement and environmental damage. The village where he grew up now lies in ruins while the families who remain there face health problems they believe are linked to contamination from decades of conflict.

As Ibrahim explores the destruction and meets affected families, he reflects on his own family, the life they might have had if he had stayed and whether they could ever return home.

Ghost Towns of Afghanistan is a documentary film by Matty Feurtado and Ibrahim Sulemen Khel.

Published On 17 Nov 2026

entries.title: UK sanctions eight Israeli construction firms over West Bank settlements
entries.summary: Settler group also sanctioned for blocking Gaza aid as foreign secretary calls for 'protecting the two-state solution'.
entries.content:
Settler group also sanctioned for blocking Gaza aid as foreign secretary calls for ‘protecting the two-state solution’.

The government of the United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and a settler group blocking aid to Gaza.

The companies affected in Tuesday’s asset freezes include Har Hevron Development Company Ltd, Hemdat Shomron Ltd and SAG (Velvel) Construction and Development Ltd, which construct and develop homes in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.

The measures were announced shortly before the final deadlines for the tenders for E1, a settlement project that would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from occupied East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of an independent state.

“Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this Government’s approach,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement. “That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.”

The government also imposed sanctions on Tzav 9, a group it said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks from delivering food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip.

Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Jonah Hull said the sanctions on Tzav 9 come after the UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office has noted that thousands of families in Gaza are in dire need of aid after “catastrophic” floods.

Britain’s relationship with Israel has deteriorated significantly over the past three years because of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as well as the Israeli government’s plans to expand settlements in the West Bank.

Israel in September threatened to close the British consulate building in East Jerusalem in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements.

British and Israeli diplomats last month reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure.

Attacks in West Bank continue

Meanwhile on Tuesday, Israeli forces carried out a series of raids and arrests in the West Bank, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

A Palestinian woman was killed in an attack on Monday night by Israeli settlers firing live ammunition at Palestinians in the area of the village of Ein ad-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho governorate, according to medical sources.

The Jericho Governmental Hospital reported that 10 Palestinians were injured by the settlers’ gunfire, including an elderly man.

Israeli soldiers also raided the Jalazone refugee camp and arrested two people in addition to arresting another person from el-Bireh after searching a home.

Troops also stormed Nablus, Tubas and the villages of Khallet al-Louza and Beit Falouh in Bethlehem governorate, raiding homes and shops and firing tear gas.

Rep. Thomas Massie Forces a New Fight for Epstein Survivors

entries.title: At the origin of France’s education protests, students refuse to give up
entries.summary: Blockades continue at some schools in the Parisian suburbs as students and teachers say little has improved.
entries.content:
Blockades continue at some schools in the Parisian suburbs, as students and teachers say little has improved in their classrooms.

Paris, France – On a cold, rainy morning in early November, students and teachers met outside the locked gates of Paul Eluard, a high school in Saint-Denis north of Paris. Some were wearing costumes. For 17-year-old Kamelia, dressing as a dinosaur helped her to maintain the joy and hope that coexisted with the anger driving the student movement in mid-September.

“Costumes are the fun part. They show that it’s not all about violence. There’s also good cheer and fun in all of this,” Kamelia told Al Jazeera. “Today there are huge protests all over France, and it’s very important. I got up early, and even though I’m a little tired, I came anyway.”

Four days after students at Paul Eluard returned from a mid-term break, they joined a national strike on November 5. Nearby, students from the trade school Bartholdi had blockaded the gates of their school. Although the size of the student protests peaked in early October, many young people, especially in the suburbs, are refusing to return to the classroom until some of their demands are met.

“Sometimes, we see rats in the courtyard and in the restrooms. The restrooms are a mess. We don’t have enough water; it flows very slowly. We don’t have enough to drink, and the restrooms are dirty. The hallways are dirty, the classrooms are dirty, and there are cockroaches,” 17-year-old Nohlan, a student at Bartholdi, told Al Jazeera outside the school’s blockade.

The movement started at a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17, and rapidly spread to Saint-Denis, then the rest of France. Students blocked the entrances to their schools to protest poor classroom conditions and took to the streets.

“The movement started in the suburbs, then Paris followed suit. Now the whole world is watching us,” Kamelia said. “[In Saint-Denis], we’re basically ignored, even though we’re part of this country. But we’re here, and we are the future of this country.”

By the end of September, an estimated 400 schools across France, including some universities, had joined the student movement. Protests on October 17 in Paris saw an estimated 550,000 participants, according to the interior minister, while organisers put the number at 800,000.

Although this is not the first time in recent years that students in working-class suburbs have protested against school conditions, the scale of this year’s movement has been remarkable.

“It really started to gain momentum, and when everyone started to get involved, it was incredible. It really moved me because last year, we set up a few blockades, but no one heard about them,” Kamelia said.

Although students are at the heart of the movement, many teachers have since joined, expressing solidarity with their students and deploring the conditions under which they have to teach.

High school students are setting the pace for the movement, said Lucie Sabze, an English teacher at Paul Eluard.

“I’m impressed by the students, their demands and their political discourse, which is very lucid and very clear,” she told Al Jazeera. “I think the scale of the movement can be explained by a growing frustration.”

Teachers at Eluard are celebrating one “victory”. They had been calling for the resignation of the head teacher, who they accused of letting an officer from France’s notoriously violent motorised antiterrorism brigade into the school to arrest a student.

On Sunday, a government agency announced Xavier Artaud had stepped down “as a safety precaution”.

“Given the unacceptable public accusations made against the high school principal by name, he requested protective measures requiring his removal from the Saint-Denis area,” said the Academic Director of National Education Services.

Bruno Gbalou, an English teacher at neighbouring Bartholdi, noted that conditions have only deteriorated in recent years.

“It’s been about 15 years since I came back from England and started teaching here, and things have only gotten worse. So there are more students, but we have fewer resources,” Bruno Gbalou told Al Jazeera. “It’s not fair to the students, and it’s not fair to us, and that’s one of the reasons why we’re going on strike.”

In a statement to the media in early October, President Emmanuel Macron said the government planned to respond to students’ demands “in the most concrete way possible”.

“I understand the anxieties, sometimes the anger, that our youth can have, whether about the climate, technological changes or geopolitical situations,” Macron said.

But the students who spoke to Al Jazeera said they do not believe the government has offered them real solutions. The November blockade at Bartholdi in Saint-Denis was in response to a lack of solutions, said student Nohlan.

“There’s still no change. We’re hoping for change, but we’re waiting, and waiting,” he said.

Louis Boyard, a member of the French National Assembly for Val-de-Marne, the administrative area where the protest movement started, explained that the government’s policies have significantly reduced educational resources.

“Macron pursued a policy of austerity, and as a result, he gradually dismantled public education while providing massive subsidies to the private sector because he supports private education over public education,” Boyard told Al Jazeera. “Macron thinks that by sweeping the problem under the rug, people will just go home. That’s not true. The people speaking out can’t really afford to eat any more. One in three French people are skipping meals. People – young people – have gone too far in this movement to back down now.”

The left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is currently polling about 20 percent in France’s upcoming presidential elections, has been accused of weaponising the student movement for political gain. But Boyard insisted that the movement was organic, and that LFI had simply followed because the party is “always on the side of those who fight”.

“Whenever there’s a struggle led by young people, I participate because I believe that young people have every right to get involved and fight,” Boyard said. “The movement took off because all the high school students looked at each other and said: ‘We’re not being respected. So we’re going to make sure we’re respected’.”

When he was a high school student, Boyard participated in a blockade, prompted by an asbestos problem, in 2018. Thanks to the protests, the students were able to get the school rebuilt.

“I’ve already won a victory this way, and we were justified in doing it. [The current students], too, are justified in doing it,” Boyard said.

As she inflated her dinosaur costume to join the protests in the centre of Paris, Kamelia wanted to send a message of hope.

“Everyone is rising up – all the young people. We’re a generation who’s truly awakened. It makes me so happy,” she said.

entries.title: Infantino’s FIFA challenger Diallo claims to have support beyond Europe
entries.summary: French football chief Philippe Diallo says he has received 'spontaneous signs of strong support' against Infantino.
entries.content:
French football chief Philippe Diallo says he has received ‘spontaneous signs of strong support’ against Infantino.

French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo says he has the backing of countries beyond Europe in his bid to depose Gianni Infantino in the upcoming FIFA presidential election.

“To beat him you need 106 votes, which is a majority,” Diallo said on Tuesday following his nomination as the European governing body UEFA’s representative.

“It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already since yesterday I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days.”

Diallo was speaking in Paris the day after accepting an invitation from UEFA to stand against Infantino in the election to be held next March.

UEFA, which has 55 member associations, said that European nations had “unanimously pledged their full support” to Diallo, ahead of Wednesday’s deadline for candidates to declare themselves.

Under its Slovenian president Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA has led the opposition to Infantino since his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors was revealed in July.

Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of widespread uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the current FIFA president in Switzerland.

Diallo announced in September that the French Football Federation (FFF) was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election, following similar announcements from other European associations. At the time he said that “the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed”.

‘Open governance’

“There can no longer be a type of single-handed governance where the biggest issues in football are decided behind the scenes, without any transparency and without anyone being consulted, without going through the executive committee,” Diallo, 63, said on Tuesday.

“My vision will be one of open, collegiate governance, in which the different bodies really play their part.”

Diallo, the 63-year-old son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the FFF since January 2023.

UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in the election, which will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat.

Arsene Wenger, the French former Arsenal manager and FIFA’s current chief of global football development, had at one point been seen as a potential candidate who could get Europe’s backing, but he will not stand.

FIFA has a total of 211 member associations, with each having one vote in the presidential election. A majority is needed for a candidate to win.
